p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: Send few texts. Too many make people leave faster than too many emails do.

Get clear written permission before you send marketing texts. In the US, the TCPA law requires it.
Put a clear way to stop (opt out) in every text.

Check the timing rules for your country before you send the three cart-reminder texts.
SMS Pump only sends texts if your account balance is at least $20.
A **win-back SMS brings back customers who have not bought for 30 days**.
Each text needs a short brand name, one **discount code**, a link, and a way to stop messages ("Reply STOP").
Keep each text under **160 characters**, or it splits into two messages.
Test SMS against email, and compare **open rate and click rate** before you do more with SMS.
When and How Much to Use SMS
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: Use SMS (text messages) **sparingly**.
People get fewer marketing texts than emails, and frequent promotions quickly annoy them. Too many texts make people opt out (stop receiving messages) faster than too many emails do.
Use SMS mainly for **valuable messages**, such as order updates. Customers want these and can opt in (say yes to receive them) on Shopify (the online store software).
Save promotional texts (texts that sell a deal) for rare, genuinely valuable offers.
Asking for SMS consent (permission to text) at checkout is fine if you might use text marketing later. Ask **very sparingly**.
Frequent discount texts can damage the customer relationship more than they help.
Email is worth **more in the long run** than a phone number, because email lets you remarket (show messages again to people who visited your website).
SMS works well when it is targeted (sent to the right person) at the right time. Still, use it sparingly.
Do **not** run ads that send visitors to an SMS sign-up page instead of your website. SMS sign-ups from paid traffic (visitors from paid ads) are not a recommended default.
Audience matters. Younger customers tend to accept text marketing more readily. Older customers may find frequent texts annoying. **Test** SMS with your audience before scaling it (making it bigger).
Collect a phone number from **every customer**, so SMS is available when it is valuable. Phone numbers are an asset for order updates and occasional offers.

Every SMS campaign should be an **automated sequence** (a series of messages sent automatically) set up early, with A/B testing (trying two versions to see which works better) built in. Never send one-off texts.
Automation captures volume even before you have large subscriber lists (lists of people who opted in).
Two sources disagree on one-off sends. says never send one-off texts. describes a one-off SMS offer update as a single setting inside a Klaviyo (email and SMS software) flow step.
Treat the one-off setting as a **step inside a flow**, not a standalone blast (one message sent to everyone).

Compliance means following the law.
Legal baseline by market
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: In the US, marketing SMS sent to customers generally needs **prior express written consent** (clear written permission given before any message) under the
TCPA (a US texting law). Every message must include a clear way to opt out. Confirm consent is captured at sign-up before running SMS flows in the US.
Before building an SMS opt-in (a sign-up for texts), **verify the required consent wording** for your jurisdiction (the country or region whose laws apply). In the US, TCPA compliance applies.
Check the SMS rules and GDPR (an EU privacy law) compliance of **every target country** before sending texts. Phone consent is stricter than email consent.
Use an SMS app with built-in compliance features, such as GDPR settings and quiet hours (times when messages must not be sent). Make sure messages are sent **only at permitted times**.
Every SMS campaign must include an **unsubscribe option** (a way to stop receiving messages).
Avoid SMS providers (the companies that send your texts) that use **shared sender numbers**, because your messages may come from a number shared with unrelated companies.
Choose a provider with a **dedicated number** (one number only for your store).
Include **opt-out instructions** in every SMS. Sending without them exposes the store to legal and carrier (phone network) complaints.
Every marketing SMS sent through SMS Bump (an SMS app) should include opt-out instructions, such as a reply STOP line (a line telling people to reply STOP).
Leaving them out creates compliance risk and hurts customer trust.
In SMS Pump (another SMS app), **always include opt-out instructions** and keep them turned on in the flow.
Opt-out and discount fields in SMS Pump: the discount code field **must be filled in** before a message is saved, and the opt-out text must have room.
Opt-In Disclosure
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: Place the disclosure (required fine print) **directly under the phone number submit button** (the button that sends the form). It must state:

that the visitor agrees to receive marketing texts,
The message frequency per month,

that message and data rates may apply (phone company charges may apply),
that consent is not a condition of purchase (the visitor does not have to say yes to buy).
Adapted from a public compliant SMS opt-in text:
By submitting this form, you agree to receive recurring automated marketing text messages (e.g. promotions and cart reminders) from [Brand Name] at the phone number provided.
Consent is not a condition of purchase. Message frequency varies (about 3 to 4 messages per month). Message and data rates may apply. Reply HELP for help or STOP to cancel.
Prompt for drafting and checking opt-in language (a prompt is a ready-made instruction you paste into an AI tool):
You are an expert in marketing and SMS law. Help me write opt-in language for a form at the bottom of a submit button on a website.
The form requires detailed opt-in language that includes marketing messages sent via SMS, about 3 to 4 messages per month, and automated messages.
When crafting the opt-in, be transparent and compliant: ask for consent, state that consent is not a condition of purchase, state the number of messages per month, and state that message
and data rates may apply. Then check my draft against the SMS disclosure language published by a major email/SMS platform and tell me where it differs.
Postscript (an SMS app) has list growth tools (Acquisitions > List growth tools > Convert your email list).
They show ready-made mobile opt-in code with TCPA-style consent language (wording that follows the US texting law). Use it as a **wording reference only**.
Check it against your own SMS provider's requirements instead of copying from a live client account.
Collecting phone numbers
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: Collect phone numbers from abandoned checkouts (customers who left before paying) and purchases,
**not through cold pop-ups (surprise boxes on a website), because phone numbers are personal. An incentive, such as an extra 5% off**, can encourage the visitor to give the number.
Collect phone numbers at checkout, where buyers already enter them. Add a second pop-up step after email signup that offers an extra **5% VIP discount** in exchange for a phone number.
The phone number field's placeholder (the grey hint text inside the box) should encourage the visitor to enter their **real number**, because the discount code is sent there.
A fake number means the visitor never receives the code and the subscriber is lost.
Name **every page** in an Optimonk (a pop-up tool) campaign before setting up navigation rules, such as the form, the email thank-you page, the SMS upgrade page and the SMS thank-you page.
Clear names keep the Next-page dropdowns (menus that pick the next page) unambiguous when a flow has several steps.
The Klaviyo SMS opt-in flow depends on the welcome flow already being live (switched on for visitors). It is complete once the **SMS opt-in flow is live**.
Trojan horse here means a two-step sign-up: first email, then SMS.
Trojan-horse structure: first collect the email with a discount reveal (a code shown after signing up), then **escalate** (step up) to an SMS upgrade with a
higher discount, so each signup leads to a bigger offer.
Set the SMS upgrade offer to **15%** (upgraded from the 10% email code) and make the upgrade the main action. Keep a 10% "No thanks" option as the alternative.

**JPEG = common photo file type. Font size = letter size. Padding = space inside a box. Margin = space outside a box. Z-index = which layer sits on top. Overlay** = dark layer behind the pop-up.

2. Cut out a lifestyle product image (a photo of the product in use) with a background-removal tool, export it as PNG, and resize it in batch (many images at once).

3. Add a Floating image element (a picture that sits over the pop-up) and drop in the resized PNG so it overlaps the top edge of the pop-up.

Add a subheadline "You've unlocked a mystery discount" (font size 30, semi-bold, with the key word in black). Semi-bold means medium-thick letters.

Setting Up SMS Bump
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: SMS Bump is the SMS-only app used here for abandoned checkout texts (reminders for people who left before paying),
post-purchase upsell texts (offers after buying) and win-back texts (messages to bring back customers who stopped buying). It can create **discount codes automatically** inside the SMS messages.
**Install SMS Bump** from the Shopify App Store (Apps > All recommended apps > Shopify app store, search "sms bump"), click Get started, and create an account.

2. When asked, choose **SMS only**, not email and SMS.
3. Enter your business information and continue.
4. On the setup page, keep the abandoned checkout flow, post-purchase upsell flow and customer win-back flow **switched on**, then click Next.
5. Finish the setup. Leave the subscription pop-up customization for later if Clavio (another pop-up tool) already runs one.
A flow is a series of automatic messages sent at set times.
1. Open Flows, scroll to Abandoned checkout, and click Edit.
2. Edit SMS 1 and change the delay (wait time) from 30 minutes to **15 minutes**. Paste the first SMS template (a ready-made text), which contains a checkout button and a reply option for questions.
3. Add SMS 2 with a delay of **2 hours**. Paste the SMS 2 template. Click the discount code field, let SMS Bump create the code automatically, and set the value to **10**.
Add the abandoned checkout URL (the link that reopens the unfinished cart) and save.
4. Click Add step, then Add delay, and choose **20 hours**. Add SMS 3 with a **20%** discount code created the same way, paste the template text and save.

5. Note on placement: if needed, remove the step and place the 20-hour delay above the SMS 2 position, then add SMS 3 with a 20 discount code.
6. Click **save**.

p.t:
1. Open SMS Pump from the App Store and click Install.
2. Click Add sales channel, then Get started.

3. Create the basic account.
4. Set up flows and campaigns inside SMS Pump.
**Balance rule: SMS Pump only sends messages if the account has a balance (prepaid money) of at least $20**.
SMS pump: abandoned checkout flow
1. Name the flow "abandoned checkout" and choose the abandoned checkout trigger (the event that starts the flow).
2. Trigger: Abandoned checkout. Add a delay of **15 minutes**, then an SMS action with the prepared text, filling in the product name in the brackets.
3. Add a condition (an if-then check): customer made an order after flow started is true. If true, end the flow; if not, continue.
4. Add a delay of **2 hours and a second SMS with a 10%** discount code created in SMS Pump.
5. Add the same condition again, then a delay of **20 hours and a third SMS offering 20% off** with an automatically generated code.
6. Make sure the discount code field is applied. If the discount amount shows red, fix it. If the opt-out text shows red, make space for it.

7. Click **Save** and confirm the flow is live.
Template for the third message (retargeting means reaching people again after they left without buying):
Hey, {product name} is still waiting in your cart, and the offer is going fast. Finish your purchase now with 20% off using the code that SMS Pump generates automatically for you: {checkout link}.
Reply STOP to opt out.

p.t: The 15-minute, 2-hour and 20-hour schedule (SMS Bump and SMS Pump) puts **three texts** within about 22 hours of abandonment.
Source E sets the first abandoned-cart SMS within **24 hours**. It says only one abandoned-cart text per customer may be sent within the first 24 hours.

Treat this as a legal limit and check the SMS marketing rules that apply in your market.
Before running the schedule, confirm it fits the rules in your market.
Abandoned checkout message design
Abandoned checkout SMS should be short, **three to four lines**.
Use the customer's first name as a dynamic field (a spot the system fills in automatically). Include the offer (10-20% off), a sense of urgency (a reason to act now) and the deal end.
Leave out reviews and extra content, since SMS must stay small and crisp.
Put the offer and the discount in the **first line** of every SMS, since readers skim and rarely read the full message. Keep messages short and direct.
Put the offer and event in the **first one or two lines** so they show in the notification (the preview on the phone screen).
A formula is a simple pattern to copy.
The pattern: a short greeting with the first name, a reminder that items are still in the cart with a note of urgency, a single checkout button, and a reply line for help.
Later messages add a discount code created in the SMS app and keep the same checkout link.
Example 1: "Hi Sam, your order is still waiting. Tap here to finish checkout before your size sells out. Reply here for help."
Example 2: "Hi Lee, your basket is saved. Here is 10% off with the code BACK10 at checkout: link. Reply STOP to opt out."
Formula: SMS retargeting (SMS pump)
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: One formula: a short reminder with the product name, a discount code that **grows with each message**,
a link straight to checkout, and an opt-out line. The delay grows over time (15 minutes, 2 hours, 20 hours), and each message offers a bigger discount than the one before.
Example A: "Hi, your [product] is still in your cart. Use code SAVE10 for 10% off, link below. Reply STOP to opt out."
Example B: "Last chance: your [product] is waiting. Take 20% off with code SAVE20 before it sells out. Reply STOP to opt out."
Open with a non-blaming line that says checkout hit a snag and the order is saved.
Then add three short proof or policy points, such as customer count, return window and free shipping threshold (the order amount needed for free shipping).
It reassures without implying carelessness and gives concrete reasons to return.
Example A: "Hiccup at checkout, don't worry, your cart is saved. 12,000 happy customers, 30-day free returns, free shipping over $75."
Example B: "Looks like checkout didn't finish, but your order is still waiting. 5,000 five-star reviews, easy 60-day exchanges, free delivery from $100."
1. Add a conditional split (the message splits into two paths based on a rule) based on **cart value** (the total of items in the cart).
2. If the cart value is **over $100**, send the variant (a second version of the message) that mentions free shipping.
3. If not, send the variant that leads with a different value proposition (the main reason to buy), such as customer count or free returns.
Abandoned checkout SMS flows work well. Use SMS and email **together** and compare their performance across campaigns.
A post-purchase upsell is an offer for a related product after the buyer has already bought.
SMS bump procedure
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: 1. Open Flows, click Edit on the post-purchase upsell flow, and open the first SMS.
2. Paste the template that thanks the buyer for the order and suggests a complementary product (an item that goes well with it).

Insert the product name of a related item, add its product page link, and include a short link version.
3. Save the first SMS.
4. Add a step with a delay of **12 hours**, then add a second SMS.
Mention the recommended product, add an optional discount code (example: 10% extra at checkout), add the checkout and product links, and a reply line for questions.

5. **Always include opt-out instructions** in each message, then save.
SMS 1 (immediately after purchase):
Hey [first name], thank you for your recent purchase of [purchased product]. We hope you are enjoying it.
We think you might also be interested in [alternative product, e.g. a ring or a necklace], which is a great complement to [purchased product] and we think you will love it.
Click here to check it out: [product page link]. If you have any questions, just reply to this message and we will be happy to help.
SMS 2 (12 hours after purchase):
Hey [first name], just wanted to remind you about the great deal we are currently offering on [recommended product].
It is a perfect complement to your product that you already purchased, and we think you will love it. Plus, use code [discount code] at checkout to save an extra 10 percent on your purchase.
Click here to check it out: [recommended product link]. If you have any questions, just reply to this message and we will be happy to help. Always include the opt-out instructions.
SMS pump procedure
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: 1. Create a new flow, choose the post-purchase upsell trigger, and add a delay of **1 hour**.
2. Add an SMS that thanks the customer for the purchase and recommends another store product as a complement. The recommended product URL is added automatically.

Include a checkout link and reply-to-message support.
3. Add the condition: customer made an order after flow started. If true, end the flow.
4. If not, add a delay of **12 hours and a second SMS reminding them of the deal, with a fixed $10** discount using the "plus use code" field. The code must be applied at checkout.
5. Make sure opt-out instructions are on, then save the flow as "product upsell sequence".
Formula: thank the buyer, name the purchased item, suggest **one** complementary product that fits with it, give the product link,
and add a short reply option. Keep the message brief and useful. Send the second reminder only after a delay so it does not feel like spam.
Example 1: "Thanks for ordering the hoodie, Ana. Many buyers add the matching beanie. See it here: link."

Example 2: "Hi Max, your speaker is on its way. Pair it with a carrying case at 10% off with code CASE10: link."
Template for SMS Pump:
Hey [first name], thanks for your recent purchase of [your product name]. We hope you are enjoying it. We noticed you might also be interested in [recommended product name].
It is a great complement to [your product name] and we think you will love it. Click here to check it out: [recommended product URL].
If you have any questions, just reply to this message and we will be happy to help. Reply STOP to opt out.
**Discount difference: SMS Bump uses an optional 10% code in the second message, while SMS Pump uses a fixed $10** code. Use the one that matches the tool you run.
Win-Back: SMS Bump procedure
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: **Trigger (the event that starts a message): Days without order**, set to **30**,

meaning 30 days since the customer's last purchase. The source describes two routes to the same setting.
Route A:
1. **Click Edit** on the customer win-back flow. A flow is an automatic series of messages. Win-back means bringing back customers who stopped buying.

2. **Remove** any extra delay step (a waiting time before the next step), so the trigger alone controls timing.
3. **Set the trigger to Days without order and enter 30**.
**Edit the SMS (text message): paste the template, create a discount code (a code the customer types at checkout to pay less) with the desired amount (example: 15% on the next purchase),**

**add the homepage link and an opt-out** instruction (a way to stop future messages).
5. **Click save.**
Route B (adds a delay, then removes it):

1. **Click edit** on the Customer win-back flow.
2. **Add a step with a delay in days set to 30**.

3. **Edit the SMS with the win-back template and create a discount code** with the chosen amount.
4. **Click save.**

5. **Remove the extra delay step, set Customer win-back with days without order to 30**, then **save**.
Template:
Hey [first name], we noticed that it has been a while since you made a purchase from our store. We miss you.
To show how much we value you, we are offering a special deal just for you: use code [discount code] at checkout to save 15 percent on your next purchase.
Click here to check out what is new: [home page link]. Hope to see you back soon. Reply STOP to opt out.
SMS Pump procedure
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: 1. **Create a new flow, choose the order created trigger (it starts when an order is placed), and add a delay of 10 days**.
2. **Add an SMS action (a step that sends a text) with the win-back text and a $15 discount code. Then add the website URL** (the web address; replace it with your store URL).
3. **Save** and name the flow "customer win back sequence".
4. **Add a delay of 30 days and a second SMS with a $15** discount or more, a new arrivals message (a text about new products), and a store link.

5. **Include** the message "we hope to see you back soon."
Template:
Hey [first name], we noticed it has been a while since your last purchase from [store name]. We miss you.
To show how much we value you, here is a special deal just for you: use code [discount code] to save $15 on your next order. Click here to see what is new: [store URL]. We hope to see you back soon.
Reply STOP to opt out.

Use this checklist for every win-back message:
Mention the **time** since the last order.

Say you **miss** the customer.
Offer a **discount** for the next purchase.
Link to **new products**.

Add an **opt-out line** (a way to stop messages).
Keep the offer **modest and specific**.
Examples:
"Hi Jo, it has been a while since your last order. Here is 15% off your next order with code COMEBACK15: link. Reply STOP to opt out."
"We have new arrivals you may like, Mia. Use code WELCOMEBACK for 15% off at checkout: link. Reply STOP to unsubscribe."
**Trigger difference:** SMS Bump uses days without order (**30**). SMS Pump uses the order-created trigger with a **10-day first delay. Both put the second message at 30 days**.
**Discount difference: SMS Bump uses a percentage (15%)**. SMS Pump uses **$15**.
VIP and Loyalty SMS
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: Confirmation for a **VIP upgrade** (moving a customer into the best-customer group):
You made it into the VIP group! Here's your bumped-up 15% discount code as promised. Tap this link to unlock it and start shopping: {DISCOUNT_LINK} Applied automatically at checkout.

Reply STOP if you'd like to unsubscribe.
The VIP phone-number step offers an extra **5% in exchange for a phone number** after email signup.
A **character is one letter, number, space or symbol.**
**The character limit** is the most characters one message can hold.
Start each SMS with the **brand name** and a colon, so the reader knows who sent it.
Keep the brand name **short**, so there is room for the offer and the link inside the character limit.
In the Klaviyo SMS editor (Klaviyo is email and SMS software, and the editor is where you write the text), turn **on** "Automatically shorten links."
Add **one blank line** before the final sentence, so the message does not look cramped.
Klaviyo's SMS editor counts characters against **160** for a single message.
Longer messages are sent as multiple parts. The counter then shows a **306-character** limit for two parts.
Shorten the text where possible, so the message stays within **one 160-character part**.
A draft with a link read **190 of 306**, which splits the message into two parts. **Check the counter** before saving.
Include a **reply line** for questions in each message, such as "If you have any questions, just reply to this message and we will be happy to help."

For a personal tone, **write as one person** who is ready to answer, not as a broadcast (a message sent the same way to many people).
A **phone number** is personal.
Campaign settings and tool checks
p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: For a **one-off SMS offer update in Klaviyo (a single change, not a repeated message), turn off** Smart Sending

and Quiet Hours in the SMS step.
Smart Sending limits how many messages one person gets. Quiet Hours stops sending at set times.
The message then sends at its **scheduled point** in the flow instead of being held.
**Source conflict:** requires quiet hours and permitted send times. turns Quiet Hours off for a one-off offer update.
Permitted send times are the hours your market's rules allow messages. **Check them** in your market before turning Quiet Hours off.

Check the **Optimonk Next-page settings (Optimonk is a pop-up tool that shows boxes on your website): Conversion closed (the visitor took the wanted action), campaign goal reached**, **Smart sync on**.
**Name every Optimonk page** before setting up navigation (the way visitors move between pop-up pages).
1. **Set up** an SMS message on the abandoned-cart flow first.
The abandoned-cart flow sends messages to customers who left items in the cart without paying.
2. **Compare the open rate (share of people who open the message), the click-through rate** (share who click the link), and purchases from SMS against the same flow in email.
3. **Expand SMS** only if it performs better or adds value your email cannot.
**Use SMS and email together** and compare their performance across campaigns (a campaign is one set of messages sent for one goal).
**Build SMS and email flows as automated sequences, with A/B testing** built in from the start (A/B testing means sending two versions to split groups to see which works better).
**Test the Optimonk pop-up live before relying on it, enabling the app embed** in the Shopify theme. Shopify is the online store platform. The theme is the store's design.
The app embed is the switch that adds an app to that design.

p.s: SMS marketing: compliance, opt-in and flows

p.t: SMS Bump and Postscript are Shopify SMS tools (apps that send text messages in a Shopify store).

They are broadly similar, so **how you use SMS matters more than which tool you pick**. Drip (an email tool) and some email autoresponders (tools that send scheduled emails automatically) also offer SMS features.
TxtCart is an SMS cart recovery app (it messages customers who left items in their cart). It is easy to set up. The author reported a **50x ROAS** during the free trial.
ROAS (return on ad spend) is money earned per dollar spent on ads, so 50x means 50 dollars back for each dollar spent.
The author said that result was strong enough that other SMS recovery apps were no longer needed. This is a **single reported trial result**, not a benchmark (a standard to compare against).
